The paper’s claims are stronger than the evidence. Phrases suggesting general, implementation-ready guidelines across robotics RL are not fully justified given the restriction to state-based observations, small MLP policies, simulation-only experiments, and a small set of algorithms.

The treatment of stochastic policies is a central unresolved issue. The authors acknowledge that projection warps the action distribution and makes log probabilities intractable, then use a practical workaround; this workaround may itself drive some conclusions and deserves more rigorous validation or alternative baselines.

Positioning relative to the closest prior work is thin. The manuscript cites related studies but does not make sufficiently precise what is fundamentally new beyond extending the empirical grid to more algorithms, rewards, and tasks.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and under-studied issue: how SO(3) action parameterizations affect deep RL, as distinct from the better-studied supervised rotation-representation setting.

The manuscript is unusually clear for this topic and provides useful practitioner guidance about local tangent-space delta actions, action scaling, unit-centering, and pitfalls with entropy and projection.

The empirical coverage is reasonably broad: PPO, SAC, and TD3; dense and sparse rewards in the idealized setting; and several robotics-style benchmarks including drones, RoboSuite, and goal-conditioned arm tasks.
The appendix contains helpful ablations and diagnostics, including noise projection visualizations, entropy effects, centering variants, 6D-vs-matrix comparisons, and scaling of tangent actions.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Much of the contribution is an empirical primer combining known SO(3) representation facts with standard RL algorithms, and the paper does not clearly separate what is new from prior work such as Geist et al. and Schuck et al.

The evaluation is not fully convincing for top-tier acceptance. Real-robotics benchmarks often use only five seeds, have large variance, and lack statistical testing; the more exhaustive 50-run analysis is mainly on an idealized toy rotation environment.

The comparisons are confounded by representation-specific implementation choices. For PPO/SAC, the paper samples in Euclidean space and relies on environment-side projection, so the policy likelihood is not the likelihood of the executed SO(3) action. This is central to the conclusions but treated as a practical compromise rather than compared against manifold-aware policy distributions or corrected objectives.

Baselines are incomplete. The paper does not compare against specialized SO(3)/Lie-group RL methods, manifold distributions, alternative exploration schemes, or prior orientation-control implementations beyond representation swaps in standard algorithms.

The robotic benchmarks are selective: only a subset of representations is evaluated, dense/sparse reward coverage is uneven, and some environments are modified/custom, weakening the claim of broad generality across standard robotics benchmarks.

Reproducibility is weaker than claimed. The project webpage/code URL appears blank in the manuscript, hyperparameter search spaces and selected values are not fully specified, and some benchmark settings are only described at a high level.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence supports, especially the broad recommendation that local tangent-space delta actions are generally best across algorithms and tasks; RoboSuite results are mixed and sometimes favor quaternions or task-specific factors.

There are technical and presentation rough edges, including notation issues around Lie algebra/tangent-space symbols, imprecise statements about covers/singularities, and minor textual/formatting problems. These do not invalidate the work but reduce confidence in polish and rigor.
